source: Bornmann, Tekles, Zhang, Ye (2019) Do we measure novelty when we analyze unusual combinations of cited references? F1000Prime validation
finding: First direct validity test of Uzzi-style score U against expert faculty judgments. Score U mostly agrees with expert 'new finding' tags. The Wang-style score W mostly does not.
numbers: n=23,206 papers in the main model. +1 SD in score U gives +7.47% expected 'new finding' tags and +58.78% for 'novel drug target'. Pseudo R2 of the main model is only 0.33%.
limits: Biomedicine only. F1000 faculty may be swayed by citations, so tags mix novelty and impact.
agent_relevance: Cited-reference atypicality has a weak but real signal for expert-rated novelty. Use it as one cheap feature, never as the judge.

source: Bornmann et al. (2019) score W result
finding: Score W (new journal pairs that later get co-cited, weighted by ease of combination) failed convergent validity. The authors advise using U and questioning W.
numbers: Only some F1000 tags matched expectations for W. Authors state: use novelty score U, question W.
limits: Same F1000 sample. A 2024 corrigendum exists (DOI 10.1016/j.joi.2024.101544); not read.
agent_relevance: Two novelty measures built on the same citation data can differ in validity. Use the validated one and say which.

source: Bornmann et al. (2019) effect sizes
finding: Effects of novelty scores on expert tags are significant but small. Keyword score K was a weak comparison metric.
numbers: Standardized coefficient for U on 'new finding' is about 0.12 SD per SD. Many tag models show single-digit percent changes. Detailed model R2 0.33%.
limits: Very small explained variance.
agent_relevance: A signal that explains under 1% of variance cannot rank candidates alone. Combine with other checks.

source: Lin, Evans, Wu (2022) New directions in science emerge from disconnection and discord
finding: Papers with atypical citation mixes are nearly twice as likely to be disruptive as conventional papers. The effect takes ten years or more to show.
numbers: Most novel vs most conventional: 61% vs 36% disruptive. Cohorts 1970 (87,475 papers), 1980 (176,826), 1990 (318,914), 2000 (591,653). Only 2.3% of papers are highly atypical; the share fell from 3.9% (1970) to 1.4% (2000).
limits: Journal-pair z-scores. The disruption index D is itself contested.
agent_relevance: Novelty pays late. A scaffold that judges ideas by quick feedback will undervalue novel ones.

source: Lin, Evans, Wu (2022) correlation sizes
finding: Correlations between atypicality and outcomes are tiny even when group differences look large.
numbers: Typicality vs disruption D: Pearson r = -0.05 (p<0.001). Atypicality vs Sleeping Beauty Index: r = 0.08 on log-log scale (p<0.001).
limits: Huge N makes tiny r significant.
agent_relevance: Group effects (61% vs 36%) and per-item predictive power (r about 0.05) are very different. Novelty scores are weak per-item predictors.

source: Lin, Evans, Wu (2022) hits versus disruption
finding: Confirms Uzzi: a mix of conventional and atypical references best predicts becoming a high-citation hit. But the chance of disrupting peaks at the highly novel end. Two outcomes want two recipes.
numbers: Fig 1c vs 1d in text; novel papers 61% disruptive vs 36% conventional.
limits: Cited-reference based; ignores text content.
agent_relevance: Define the target first: reliable good (tradition plus a little novelty) or rare breakthrough (go far). Open mode can switch the target.

source: Lin, Evans, Wu (2022) embedding reformulation
finding: The atypicality z-score can be rebuilt as distance between journal embeddings, which is cheaper and tracks time.
numbers: Embedding inner product vs z-score: Pearson r = 0.74 (p<0.001). Embedding spaces: 1970 (2,429 journals), 2000 (8,009 journals).
limits: r = 0.74 shares about 55% of variance; not a perfect proxy.
agent_relevance: Embedding distance is a workable novelty proxy for an LLM agent, with about 45% unexplained variance.

source: Uzzi, Mukherjee, Stringer, Jones (2013) Atypical combinations and scientific impact (as quoted by Bornmann 2019 and Lin 2022)
finding: Founding study of 17.9 million papers. Highest-impact work mixes mostly conventional journal pairs with a tail of atypical ones.
numbers: Quoted: papers with high tail novelty and high median conventionality have nearly twice the propensity to be unusually highly cited (17.9M papers, all fields).
limits: Second-hand quote only; original not read. Journal-pair z-scores.
agent_relevance: Basis for the 'mostly familiar plus a small surprise' rule. Correlational.

source: Wang, Veugelers, Stephan (2017) Bias against novelty in science (as summarised in Bornmann 2019)
finding: Highly novel papers are cited less at first and more after several years. They also seed big follow-on work.
numbers: As quoted: novel papers are 'more likely to become a big hit' and to stimulate high-impact follow-ons. Exact odds not read.
limits: Second-hand. Uses new journal pairs (score W), which failed convergent validity in Bornmann 2019.
agent_relevance: Early scoring penalises novelty. Do not kill novel candidates on first-look feedback.

source: Mairesse & Pezzoni (2018) novelty and citations of French scientists (as cited by Bornmann 2019)
finding: Independent data on French scientists agree with Wang 2017: novelty shows up in citations only in the long run.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Second-hand.
agent_relevance: One partial independent confirmation of the delayed-payoff pattern.

source: Kim, Cerigo, Jeong, Youn (2016) Technological novelty profile and invention's future impact
finding: Uzzi-style z-scores applied to US patent class pairs. Patenting is getting more conventional over time. Novelty on top of a conventional base earns more citations.
numbers: 8,884,909 utility patents to Dec 2014; 80.3% have 2+ codes. High impact = top 5% of 5-year citations within a year. High median-z has a small positive effect.
limits: Patent classes, not text. Citations as impact proxy. Panel (b) detail not fully read.
agent_relevance: The Uzzi pattern carries over to patents. Novelty works as a spice on a conventional base.

source: He & Chen (2018) Predictive effects of novelty measured by temporal embeddings on growth of scientific literature
finding: A text-embedding novelty measure (semantic change of terms) predicts later growth of a topic, with effects lasting more than ten years.
numbers: MEDLINE/PubMed panel 1996-2005; 713,912 observations, mean one-step growth 4.63%, SD 22.13%. Random-effects panel models for t+1 to t+10.
limits: Predicts topic growth, not paper quality.
agent_relevance: A citation-free, text-based novelty score exists and predicts something real, which suits an LLM agent with no citation data.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas? Large-scale human study
finding: In blind expert review, LLM ideas were rated more novel than human expert ideas.
numbers: 49 expert writers, 79 reviewers, 298 unique reviews. Novelty mean: human 4.84 (n=119), AI 5.64 (n=109, p<0.01), AI plus human rerank 5.81 (p<0.001).
limits: Ideas only, not executed. Style was normalised by an LLM; humans got 50% accuracy telling AI from human ideas.
agent_relevance: Generation is not the bottleneck; selection is.

source: Si et al. (2024) trade-offs and reviewer agreement
finding: AI ideas win on novelty and excitement but not on feasibility. Expert reviewers agree only weakly.
numbers: Excitement human 4.55 vs AI 5.19 (p<0.05). Feasibility human 6.61 vs AI 6.34 (n.s.). Inter-reviewer agreement 56.1% vs 66.0% (NeurIPS 2021) and 71.9% (ICLR 2024 LM papers); chance 50%.
limits: PhD-level NLP reviewers; noisy gold standard.
agent_relevance: Even human novelty labels are noisy (56% agreement), so any novelty check built on them has a low ceiling.

source: Si et al. (2024) LLM-as-judge
finding: LLM reviewers are weak: the best pairwise setup reached only 71.4% on accepted-vs-rejected papers.
numbers: Claude-3.5-Sonnet 71.4% accuracy; human idea-review agreement 56.1%.
limits: Task is quality, not novelty alone.
agent_relevance: Do not let the model grade its own novelty. Matches the guardrail against self-grading.

source: Sinhahajari, Majumder, Poria (2026) On the limits of LLM-as-judge for scientific novelty (RQ-Bench)
finding: LLM judges rate LLM-written research questions as highly novel (a 'novelty mirage'). Domain experts prefer author-anchored questions.
numbers: gpt-5.5 non-obviousness win vs reference: 27.2% standalone, 49.1% comparative (tie 59.1% to 36.8%). Human experts gave the reference win rates of 78% and 56%; LLM judges gave gpt-5.5 82% and 52%. Human-LLM agreement as low as 22%; expert-expert 60%, LLM-LLM 52%.
limits: Expert study on 50 items; two LLM judges.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence against LLM self-judged novelty. Side-by-side judging inflates the effect by breaking ties toward model output.

source: Sinhahajari et al. (2026) narrowness fix
finding: Asking LLM judges explicitly to rate narrowness or source-boundedness recovers agreement with experts' non-obviousness view.
numbers: gpt-5.5 source-bound lose rate 71.7% standalone to 85.4% comparative; diagnostic-framing lose rate 2.9% to 53.4%. Gemini approved 98% of extracted reference RQs; humans 100% of 50 sampled.
limits: Small human sample (50).
agent_relevance: Add a counted 'narrow or source-bound?' check. A named dimension catches what a generic 'novel?' prompt misses.

source: Schopf & Farber (2026) RINoBench: Is this idea novel?
finding: LLMs fail to reproduce human novelty grades even though their reasoning text sounds like the human rationale.
numbers: 1,381 research ideas with expert labels. Best macro-F1 17.2 (GPT-5), o3 16.2. F1 = 0.0 for the 'not novel' class in every model. Reasoning models only slightly ahead.
limits: 5-point rubric, zero-shot prompting; GPT-4.1 scored the justification metrics.
agent_relevance: LLMs almost never say 'not novel'. A novelty check needs a forced prior-art search, not a feeling.

source: Wu et al. (2026) NovBench: LLMs on paper novelty assessment
finding: 11 general LLMs and several review-fine-tuned models show limited understanding of novelty; fine-tuned review models often fail to follow instructions.
numbers: 1,684 paper-review pairs from an NLP conference. Best average Relevance 3.6983 (zero-shot). Few-shot raised Coverage and Correctness at some cost elsewhere.
limits: Four-part rubric partly LLM-scored; NLP papers only.
agent_relevance: Fine-tuning on peer reviews did not fix novelty judgment. Scaffold-level fixes look more promising than training.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) NovGauge: fine-grained novelty benchmark
finding: Splitting novelty into task, problem and method shows models hallucinate evidence and give reasons that do not support their verdict.
numbers: 619 paper pairs, 50 multi-paper sets, 18 LLMs. Hallucination 0% to 39%. Mismatch flags 72.5% of correct positives. Only 5 of 54 model-dimension cells keep half their raw F1. GPT-5.5 verified F1 43-72%; keeps 84% of F1 on task but 55% on method.
limits: ICLR overlap claims as labels; the mismatch judge is also an LLM.
agent_relevance: Require verbatim evidence spans checked by code. Method novelty is hardest to ground.

source: Tan et al. (2025) HSPIM: hierarchical LLM paper innovation measure
finding: Splitting a paper into sections and questions, then aggregating confidence-weighted scores, beats one-shot full-paper prompting and supervised baselines.
numbers: RMSE down 35.4% (0.916 to 0.592) for DeepSeek and 17.3% (0.770 to 0.634) for GPT vs one-step zero-shot. 6.2% better than a supervised Transformer. HSPIM+ RMSE 0.4533, MAE 0.3917.
limits: Target is reviewer novelty scores on conference papers; the paper notes citations do not track innovation cleanly.
agent_relevance: Decomposed, counted aggregation helps novelty scoring. Fits 'program counts, model fills slots'.

source: Shahid et al. (2025) Literature-grounded novelty assessment of scientific ideas
finding: Retrieving related papers plus facet re-ranking gives about 13% higher agreement with experts than prior approaches. Dropping retrieval parts cuts accuracy sharply.
numbers: 'Not novel' accuracy: complete system 89.66%; without relevance RankGPT 13.79%; without embedding filtering 10.34%; without snippet retrieval 8.62%; keyword only 5.17%. Zero-shot LLM accuracy 0.68, F1 0.65.
limits: Small expert-annotated set; GPT-4o in 2024.
agent_relevance: Grounding in retrieved prior art is what makes novelty judgment work.

source: Veugelers & Wang (2019) Scientific novelty and technological impact (cited in NovBench and Bornmann; not read)
finding: Cited as showing novel papers have higher technological (patent) impact. Details not read.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Second-hand mention.
agent_relevance: Open lead for patent-side evidence.

source: Crossref record: New and atypical combinations: an assessment of novelty and interdisciplinarity (Research Policy 2020)
finding: Metadata only. Compares novelty and interdisciplinarity measures built on atypical combinations. Content not read.
numbers: Crossref cited-by count 109 at query time.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Lead for testing that novelty and interdisciplinarity are different constructs.

source: Fleming (2001) Recombinant uncertainty in technological search (cited in Bornmann 2019; not read)
finding: Cited as the early patent study of novel combinations. From memory: new combinations raise outcome variance and lower the average usefulness of inventions. Not verified this session.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: From memory plus citation context; unverified.
agent_relevance: Supports a risk framing: novelty raises variance, so a selector must tolerate failures.

source: Lin et al. (2022) Table S1 field check
finding: The disruptive-vs-developing asymmetry for novel papers is tested inside 11 fields of the 1970 cohort only.
numbers: 45,677 of 87,475 1970 papers (52%) matched to fields; 11 fields with 100+ papers.
limits: Half the cohort matched; a single cohort.
agent_relevance: Field generality is only partly shown; treat as unproven.

source: Synthesis across opened studies: weak validity picture
finding: Citation-based novelty has modest validity: R2 under 1% against expert tags, r near 0.05-0.08 against outcomes, score W failed validation. LLM direct grading is worse. No large preregistered replication of Uzzi 2013 was found this session.
numbers: R2 0.33% (Bornmann); r -0.05 and 0.08 (Lin); best macro-F1 17.2 (RINoBench).
limits: Outcome definitions differ across studies; search tools were rate-limited so the replication hunt was incomplete.
agent_relevance: Treat the 'nearly twice' result as correlational and moderate. Use novelty signals as weak features inside a retrieval-grounded, code-checked selection step.
